headings.text: Definition of safety in the EU
How do we make a cobot safe and productive?
Can an application be fully safe?

html:
The big picture

Human-robot interaction (HRI) covers every situation where robots and people meet, in steps of increasing closeness: sharing a space (coexistence), working on a task together (collaboration), communicating (interaction) and touching (physical interaction). It is multidisciplinary — robotics, computer science and the human sciences. As soon as humans are near a machine, safety (avoiding accidents) dominates, distinct from security (preventing crime). In the EU safety is set by directives and standards (ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066 for cobots), which define four collaborative operation modes. Measures follow the hierarchy of controls — remove the hazard first, protective equipment last — and risks are found and ranked systematically, e.g. with FMEA. The central lesson: a robot is never safe on its own; only an application can be made safe. Beyond safety, HRI raises questions of bias and ethics.

Content

  • What is human-robot interaction (HRI)?
  • Forms of HRI / applications
  • Safety and safety in robotics
  • Open (research) issues and achievements
  • "Exotic" forms of HRI
  • Ethical questions

What is human-robot interaction?

  • A robot and a human share a (work)place — coexistence, +
  • they do something together — collaboration, +
  • they communicate with each other — interaction, +
  • they communicate by physical contact — physical interaction.
  • Cobot: collaborative robot.
  • Pictured: a humanoid service robot (Aldebaran – United Robotics Group), cobot arms (Universal Robots, Hebi Robotics), a service robot in a restaurant in Klagenfurt.
Intuition

The "+" signs mean each level includes the ones before it. A cleaning robot in an office coexists with people (same space, separate tasks). A cobot that holds a part while a worker screws it on collaborates. A receptionist robot that answers questions interacts. A rehabilitation robot that moves a patient's arm has physical interaction. The closer the level, the harder the safety problem.

HRI is a multidisciplinary challenge

HRI sits where three fields overlap: robotics (engineering, real-world environments, uncertainty and noise), computer science (AI, machine learning, computer vision) and interacting with humans (psychology, sociology, design). Source: Sarah Sebo and Valerie Zhao, Introduction to HRI.

Forms of HRI

Application areas: healthcare, education, manufacturing, homes and elder-care facilities, food delivery, shopping-mall assistance — and many more.

Safety in robotics

  • Whenever a machine and a human share a common place, safety becomes a very important issue.
  • Think of robots as autonomous cars without the possibility of human intervention — similarly, larger robots can transmit lethal forces.

Asimov's "three laws" of robotics (from a science-fiction story — I. Asimov, Runaround, Astounding Science Fiction, March 1942):

  1. A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
  2. A robot must obey the orders given to it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
  3. A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.
Common mistake

Treating Asimov's laws as a design rule for real robots. They are a plot device — the stories are about how they fail. A real robot can't evaluate "harm" or "through inaction" in general; real safety is engineered from measurable limits (speeds, forces, distances, stop times) set in standards, as below.

Safety and security

  • Isn't there another term, "security"? What is the difference?
  • Safety: accident avoidance.
  • Security: crime prevention.
  • Examples?
Worked example — sorting examples into safety and security
  1. A cobot pinches a worker's hand because a sensor drifted → safety (no intent, an accident).
  2. An attacker changes a robot's speed limits over the network → security (deliberate act). Note it causes a safety problem: security failures can become safety failures.
  3. A light curtain stops the robot when someone walks into the cell → safety measure.
  4. Password-protecting the robot controller and encrypting its network traffic → security measure.

Test question: is there someone trying to cause the harm? Yes → security; no → safety.

Accidents

Real incidents shown on the slides: a chess robot breaking a seven-year-old's finger (Moscow, 2022); a patient who died after robot-assisted surgery (Newcastle); a factory robot malfunction injuring a worker (China); a lawsuit over a robot accident at Tesla's Fremont factory (2025); a viral video of a Unitree humanoid robot "going berserk" (2025); a delivery robot colliding with a pedestrian (West Hollywood). "Or just search video platforms for 'robot accident'."

Safety perception of new technologies

  • Whenever a new technology emerges, safety concerns are always discussed: self-driving vehicles, aeroplanes vs. cars, AI, vaccinations.
  • By looking at this chart, which transportation method would you avoid?

Passenger deaths per 100 million passenger miles, United States, 2007–2021: passenger vehicles about 0.46–0.66; buses and trains mostly below 0.1; scheduled airlines almost zero. Source: injuryfacts.nsc.org.

Why do people fear flying, or robots, more than driving — against the numbers?

Perceived risk is not measured risk. People rate a risk higher when it is unfamiliar, out of their control, and produces rare but dramatic accidents that get media coverage — a plane crash, a robot "attacking" someone. Driving is familiar and feels controlled, so its much higher death rate per mile is underweighted. For robotics this means acceptance depends on more than statistics: a cobot must be safe and feel safe, or people will refuse it or work around it. The slides list "public acceptance" as part of risk quantification for this reason.

Definition of safety in the EU

  • European directives (Machinery Directive, …) → laws, needed for the CE marking.

  • Safety standards / technical specifications:

    • Industrial (new in 2025):

      • ISO 10218-1:2025 and 10218-2:2025, Robotics — Safety requirements (industrial robots; industrial robot applications and robot cells).
      • ISO/TS 15066, Robots and robotic devices — Collaborative robots → four operation modes for cobots.
    • Personal care: ISO 13842, Robots and robotic devices — Safety requirements for personal care robots.

    • Medical:

      • ISO 14971, Medical devices — Application of risk management to medical devices.
      • IEC 80601-2-78, Medical electrical equipment — Part 2-78: Particular requirements for basic safety and essential performance of medical robots for rehabilitation, assessment, compensation or alleviation.
Unclear (slide 11)

The personal-care standard is printed as "ISO 13842". Its number is ISO 13482 (ISO 13482:2014, Robots and robotic devices — Safety requirements for personal care robots) — digits swapped.

Operation modes for industrial cobots (ISO/TS 15066)

  1. Safety-rated monitored stop — the robot enforces a low-level stop once a human enters the collaborative cell.
  2. Hand guiding ("RC", robot teaching, etc.) — needs a guiding device with an emergency-stop switch.
  3. Speed and separation monitoring — the human's pose must be monitored; the robot must stop if the human gets too close.

  4. Power and force limiting —

    • reduce the motor torque (current) so that potential collision forces and pressures (force per area) stay below limits (different values for each body region);
    • collisions with the head are not allowed;
    • the robot is still allowed to operate;
    • but do you want to work with a robot that is allowed to (un)intentionally hurt you?
Worked example — matching a scenario to the operation mode
  1. A worker walks in to refill a parts bin; the robot freezes until they leave, then continues → safety-rated monitored stop.
  2. A technician grabs the robot's handle and drags it through a welding path to teach it → hand guiding.
  3. A laser scanner slows the robot as someone approaches and stops it at 0.5 m → speed and separation monitoring.
  4. A cobot and a worker assemble side by side; if the arm bumps the worker's forearm, the contact force stays below the forearm limit → power and force limiting.

Tell-tale: modes 1–3 avoid contact (stop, guide, keep distance); only mode 4 allows contact and limits its consequences.

Why does power and force limiting use pressure as well as force?

The same force hurts much more through a small area: p = F/A. A cobot edge or gripper finger pressing with 100 N on a few square millimetres can cut or bruise, while 100 N spread over a padded flat surface is harmless. So the limits cover both — force and pressure — and they differ by body region because tissue tolerance differs (a hand tolerates more than the face, and head contact is excluded entirely). That's also why cobots have rounded, padded shapes.

Hierarchy of safety measures

Hierarchy of controls (NIOSH), from most to least effective: elimination (physically remove the hazard), substitution (replace the hazard), engineering controls (isolate people from the hazard), administrative controls (change the way people work), PPE (protect the worker with personal protective equipment).

Why is PPE the least effective level?

Each level down depends more on people behaving correctly every time. Eliminating a hazard works even if everyone is careless; a guard (engineering) works as long as nobody removes it; a rule (administrative) works only if followed; protective gloves work only if worn, fitting, and strong enough — and they don't reduce the hazard, they just stand in its way. So you go down the pyramid only for the risk that remains after the higher levels.

How do we make a cobot safe and productive?

  • First of all: a robot/cobot itself is never safe — only a specific application can be made safe.

    • A hair dryer is also safe, but only if used as intended.

  • Understand the full application scenario:

    • Who/what participants are there (robots; humans — adults, children, trained professionals or "everyday" people)? What capabilities do they have?
    • What are the influences of the environment, and what to do when they change unexpectedly?
    • What is the specific task to be accomplished?
    • What is done by whom?
    • What information needs to be passed between participants?
    • And most importantly: how should it be engineered so that (almost) no human participant gets annoyed working with the robot? Annoyed people are more likely to try to bypass safety measures.
Intuition

"Safe robot" is like "safe knife": the same cobot is harmless placing chocolates and dangerous carrying a sharp blade at head height. Safety is a property of the robot plus tool, task, workspace, people and procedures. That is why certification is done for an application (a robot cell), and why changing the gripper or the task means redoing the risk assessment.

Can an application be fully safe?

  • If your application is "fully safe": congratulations — but can you really be sure?

  • Not all risks can be covered, or can they?

    • What to do in case of an alien attack? (Slim chances of that happening, though.)
    • Is your system safe from outside (hacking) and inside (goofing around) intrusion?
    • Is your system stable over a long time (mechanical wear, sensor drift, maintenance cycles)?

  • Risk analysis and reliability engineering, e.g. FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis):

    • identify risks;
    • quantify their importance (chance of occurrence and detection, severity) + public acceptance (death by ground vs. air traffic);
    • if the risk is too high → countermeasures.
  • If something goes wrong, who is to blame?
Worked example — ranking two failure modes with an FMEA risk priority number

In FMEA each failure mode gets three ratings, typically from 1 to 10: severity S (how bad), occurrence O (how likely), detection D (how hard to notice before it causes harm — 10 = practically undetectable). The risk priority number is \mathrm{RPN} = S \cdot O \cdot D.

  1. Failure A — emergency-stop button fails: S = 9, O = 2 (rare, tested part), D = 3 (checked every shift) → \mathrm{RPN} = 54.
  2. Failure B — proximity sensor slowly drifts: S = 6, O = 5, D = 7 (drift is gradual and silent) → \mathrm{RPN} = 210.
  3. Rank and act: B gets countermeasures first — e.g. a daily self-test against a reference target, which lowers D.

Lesson: a less severe failure can deserve more attention if it is common and hard to detect. (Many methods additionally treat any very high severity as critical regardless of the RPN.)

Active measures

  • Just shut down the robot → but that would be neither productive nor very interactive.
  • Ubiquitous sensing of the robot and its surroundings.
  • Human monitoring (also with the help of AI).
  • Active collision avoidance (path planning and human motion prediction).
  • Extensive testing (with real people) — think of Murphy's "law": "everything that can go wrong, will go wrong".
  • Simulation to reduce real-life experiment effort.
  • Digital twin for continuous monitoring (expected vs. actual behaviour).
Connection

These measures rely on the proximity, force/torque and vision sensors of 2 Sensors, and on the command priorities from 4 Operation, Simulation and Communication of Robots — hard-wired safety always wins over automation. Simulation and digital twins were introduced there too.

Application video

Courtesy of project CapSize (AAU, Sensors and Actuators group — sensors in robotics): https://www.aau.at/intelligente-systemtechnologien/sensors-and-actuators/forschung/sensoren-in-der-robotik/capsize/

Example

Consider the "hierarchy of controls" pyramid applied to a cobot workcell (photo: a person working at a cobot table). What are examples for each level?

Worked example — the hierarchy of controls for a cobot workcell (slide 18)
  1. Elimination: redesign the task so the human doesn't need to enter the robot's reach at all (e.g. parts are fed by a conveyor instead of by hand).
  2. Substitution: replace the hazard with a smaller one — a lighter, slower cobot instead of a heavy industrial arm, a soft gripper instead of a sharp tool.
  3. Engineering controls: fences, light curtains, laser scanners for speed and separation monitoring, force limiting, enabling switches.
  4. Administrative controls: training, operating procedures, warning signs, lock-out procedures during maintenance, only trained personnel in the cell.
  5. PPE: safety glasses, protective gloves, safety shoes.

Bias or discrimination?

  • Example: the "racist soap dispenser at Facebook office" — an automatic dispenser that works for a light-skinned hand but not for a dark-skinned one (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YJjv_OeiHmo; also recommended: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eUaJ9Q7OM3I).
  • Can you think of other examples? Why does this happen? How can this be avoided?
Why does a soap dispenser "discriminate", and how is it avoided?

Many such dispensers use an infrared LED and a light sensor: a hand reflects the light back and triggers the pump. Darker skin reflects less of it, so with a threshold tuned only on light-skinned testers the reflection stays below the trigger level. Nobody intended it — the bias came from who was in the test group. The same mechanism hits face detection or speech recognition trained on unbalanced data. Avoiding it: test and train with users who represent everyone who will use the product, and treat failure rates per group as a requirement, not an afterthought.

Open research topics

  • Human detection, tracking and differentiation from (moving) objects — already very good progress in lab conditions → mass crowds.
  • More sophisticated tasks: health and elderly care (e.g. dressing).
  • More realistic real-time simulation.
  • Real-time contact pressure / force estimation.
  • Verbal and non-verbal communication (with AI).
  • Reading and understanding human emotions (again with AI).
  • …

Achievements / literature

  • Achievements in HRI can be found everywhere:

    • assistive humanoid robots in hospitals, shopping centres, airports …;
    • collaborative, fenceless workplaces;
    • smart robots/cobots with onboard sensors (force/torque + proximity sensors);
    • we are able to detect humans and track them in the vicinity of the robot.
  • For more information on HRI: human-robot-interaction.org (free-to-download book).

More "exotic" forms of HRI

  • Lovotics (love and robotics) — Dr. Hooman Samani, University of the Arts London: sharing emotions through robotic devices (http://www.lovotics.com/).
  • HuggieBot 2.0 — Dr. Alexis Block et al., Max Planck Institute (Germany): building a "huggable" robot to share emotions with (https://hi.is.mpg.de/research_projects/huggiebot-2-0-a-more-huggable-robot/).

Ethics in HRI

  • What are the moral limits of robotic applications?

    • Should a robot look and behave like a human being?
    • Robotic warfare.
    • (How) do robots / smart devices affect human-human interaction and relationships?
  • At the moment clear laws are missing, and it is (and probably will be, at least for some time) an ethical question to ask yourself.

Key take-aways

  • HRI (like any topic in robotics) is multidisciplinary.
  • Interaction between machines and humans always needs extensive safety measures.
  • A robot is never safe; only the application we put it in can be made "safe".
  • Consider ethical concerns during development.
  • Only use robots for good purposes.
Connection

Bias from unrepresentative data is a general machine-learning problem — it comes back in 10 Introduction to AI.
